title: The Hodgkin-Huxley equations in plain text
text:
CHAPTER 5. THE ACTION POTENTIAL
SECTION 5.2. THE HODGKIN-HUXLEY EQUATIONS IN PLAIN TEXT

Goal of this section

In this section we write down the Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) model completely, explain where each term comes from, and see how it generates action potentials. We then simulate it with a short program and look at what the simulation shows. If you have taken a course in ordinary differential equations or control systems, you have all the mathematics you need.

A note on conventions. Hodgkin and Huxley's original 1952 paper defined voltage as the displacement from the resting potential, with depolarization negative, which was the convention of their time. Modern textbooks use the absolute membrane potential V (inside minus outside), with depolarization positive and rest near -65 mV. We use the modern convention throughout. The parameter values below are the standard modern restatement of the HH squid axon model at 6.3 degrees C, the temperature of many of their experiments.

The membrane equation

Start from the equivalent circuit of section 2.3: a membrane capacitance in parallel with three conductance branches, each with its battery.

  C_m * dV/dt = I_ext - I_Na - I_K - I_L

with

  I_Na = g_Na_max * m^3 * h * (V - E_Na)
  I_K  = g_K_max  * n^4     * (V - E_K)
  I_L  = g_L               * (V - E_L)

Parameters (per square centimeter of membrane):

  C_m      = 1 uF/cm2
  g_Na_max = 120 mS/cm2
  g_K_max  = 36 mS/cm2
  g_L      = 0.3 mS/cm2
  E_Na     = +50 mV
  E_K      = -77 mV
  E_L      = about -54.4 mV

Currents are in microamperes per square centimeter (uA/cm2), voltages in millivolts, time in milliseconds. With these units, C_m * dV/dt in uF/cm2 times mV/ms gives uA/cm2, so everything is consistent.

The leak current I_L lumps together everything else (chloride and other small conductances). E_L is chosen so that the resting potential comes out at -65 mV.

The gating variables

The heart of the model is the description of how the sodium and potassium conductances change. Hodgkin and Huxley introduced three dimensionless variables, m, h, and n, each between 0 and 1.

- n is the potassium activation variable. The potassium conductance is g_K_max * n^4.
- m is the sodium activation variable, and h is the sodium inactivation variable. The sodium conductance is g_Na_max * m^3 * h.

They interpreted these as probabilities. Imagine that a potassium "pore" opens only when four independent gating particles are all in the "permissive" position, each with probability n. Then the fraction of open pores is n^4. Similarly, a sodium pore needs three activation particles in the permissive position (probability m each) and one inactivation particle not blocking (probability h), giving m^3 * h. Why powers of 4 and 3? Because these powers gave the best fit to the S-shaped (sigmoidal) delay in the rise of conductance after a voltage step. A single first-order process would rise exponentially with no delay; raising it to a power produces a delayed sigmoidal rise. It is remarkable that later molecular studies found that voltage-gated potassium channels are indeed made of four subunits, and voltage-gated sodium channels have four similar domains, though the correspondence between the HH exponents and channel structure is not exact, and real gating is more complex.

Each gating variable x (where x is m, h, or n) obeys a first-order linear ODE at fixed voltage:

  dx/dt = alpha_x(V) * (1 - x) - beta_x(V) * x

Think of each gating particle as flipping between a non-permissive state (probability 1 - x) and a permissive state (probability x). alpha_x(V) is the rate constant for flipping to permissive, and beta_x(V) the rate constant for flipping back. Both depend on voltage.

This equation can be rewritten as

  dx/dt = (x_inf(V) - x) / tau_x(V)

with

  x_inf(V) = alpha_x(V) / (alpha_x(V) + beta_x(V))
  tau_x(V) = 1 / (alpha_x(V) + beta_x(V))

At a fixed voltage, x relaxes exponentially toward its steady-state value x_inf with time constant tau_x. This is exactly the behavior of a first-order low-pass filter. Under voltage clamp, this is why conductances change smoothly after a step.

The rate functions

Hodgkin and Huxley fitted empirical formulas for alpha and beta to their voltage clamp data. In the modern convention (V in mV, rates in 1/ms):

  alpha_m(V) = 0.1 * (V + 40) / (1 - exp(-(V + 40) / 10))
  beta_m(V)  = 4 * exp(-(V + 65) / 18)

  alpha_h(V) = 0.07 * exp(-(V + 65) / 20)
  beta_h(V)  = 1 / (1 + exp(-(V + 35) / 10))

  alpha_n(V) = 0.01 * (V + 55) / (1 - exp(-(V + 55) / 10))
  beta_n(V)  = 0.125 * exp(-(V + 65) / 80)

(At V = -40 and V = -55, alpha_m and alpha_n have the form 0/0. The limits are finite: alpha_m(-40) = 1 and alpha_n(-55) = 0.1. Numerical code should handle these points, though in practice a simulation rarely hits them exactly.)

These formulas are not derived from first principles; they are curve fits. But their general shape has a physical interpretation. If gating particles carry charge and move across the membrane's electric field, then by Boltzmann statistics, the rates should depend exponentially on voltage. The formulas have roughly this exponential character.

What the rate functions imply

It is useful to describe the behavior of x_inf and tau_x qualitatively:

- m_inf(V) rises steeply from near 0 at rest to near 1 at strongly depolarized voltages. tau_m is very short, a fraction of a millisecond. So m follows voltage almost instantly.
- h_inf(V) does the opposite: near 0.6 at rest, falling to near 0 at depolarized voltages. tau_h is several milliseconds, much slower than tau_m.
- n_inf(V) rises with depolarization, like m_inf, but tau_n is several milliseconds, so n lags behind.

So we have one fast variable (m) and two slow variables (h and n). Upon depolarization, m increases rapidly, opening sodium conductance. Then h decreases and n increases more slowly, closing sodium conductance and opening potassium conductance. This difference in time scales is the essence of the action potential.

At the resting potential of -65 mV, the steady-state values are approximately m = 0.05, h = 0.6, and n = 0.32. So the resting sodium conductance is 120 * 0.05^3 * 0.6, which is about 0.01 mS/cm2, and the resting potassium conductance is 36 * 0.32^4, which is about 0.37 mS/cm2. Potassium dominates at rest, as the GHK analysis in chapter 2 suggested.

The complete model

The HH model is a four-dimensional system of nonlinear ODEs:

  C_m * dV/dt = I_ext - g_Na_max*m^3*h*(V - E_Na) - g_K_max*n^4*(V - E_K) - g_L*(V - E_L)
  dm/dt = alpha_m(V)*(1 - m) - beta_m(V)*m
  dh/dt = alpha_h(V)*(1 - h) - beta_h(V)*h
  dn/dt = alpha_n(V)*(1 - n) - beta_n(V)*n

This is the "space-clamped" or "membrane" version, describing a patch of membrane at uniform voltage. For a propagating action potential along an axon, we must add a term for current flowing along the axon, which turns the first equation into a partial differential equation in space and time. We cover that in section 5.3.

A minimal simulation

Here is a simple Python program that simulates the HH model with the forward Euler method. (The step size of 0.01 ms is small enough for this model; for serious work, use a better integrator.) It is written in plain text; you can type it into a file and run it.

  import numpy as np

  def rates(V):
      am = 0.1*(V+40)/(1-np.exp(-(V+40)/10))
      bm = 4*np.exp(-(V+65)/18)
      ah = 0.07*np.exp(-(V+65)/20)
      bh = 1/(1+np.exp(-(V+35)/10))
      an = 0.01*(V+55)/(1-np.exp(-(V+55)/10))
      bn = 0.125*np.exp(-(V+65)/80)
      return am, bm, ah, bh, an, bn

  def simulate(I_ext, T=200.0, dt=0.01):
      V = -65.0
      am, bm, ah, bh, an, bn = rates(V)
      m, h, n = am/(am+bm), ah/(ah+bh), an/(an+bn)   # start at steady state
      trace = []
      for step in range(int(T/dt)):
          am, bm, ah, bh, an, bn = rates(V)
          INa = 120*m**3*h*(V-50)
          IK  = 36*n**4*(V+77)
          IL  = 0.3*(V+54.387)
          V += dt*(I_ext - INa - IK - IL)       # C_m = 1
          m += dt*(am*(1-m) - bm*m)
          h += dt*(ah*(1-h) - bh*h)
          n += dt*(an*(1-n) - bn*n)
          trace.append(V)
      return np.array(trace)

When I ran this program (with a simple spike counter added) for 1 second of simulated time with different constant injected currents, the results were:

- With I_ext = 0, the membrane stays at rest, about -65 mV.
- With I_ext = 2 uA/cm2, the membrane depolarizes slightly to about -60 mV and stays there: no spike. The input is subthreshold.
- With I_ext = 5 uA/cm2, the model fires a single spike at the start of the current step and then settles to a steady depolarized level without further spikes.
- With I_ext of about 6.5 uA/cm2 or more, the model fires repetitively. At 6.5 uA/cm2 it fired about 56 spikes in one second; at 10 uA/cm2 about 69; at 20 uA/cm2 about 87; and at 50 uA/cm2 about 117.
- Each spike peaks at about +40 mV, and the afterhyperpolarization reaches about -75 mV, close to E_K.

These numbers depend on the details of the integration and the definition of a spike, but they reveal a characteristic property of the HH model: when it starts to fire repetitively, it does so at a fairly high rate (here around 50 to 60 spikes per second) rather than starting from arbitrarily low rates. There is a minimum firing rate. Neurons that behave this way are classified as "type II" excitability, a classification introduced by Alan Hodgkin in 1948 based on crab axons. "Type I" neurons, like many cortical pyramidal cells, can fire at arbitrarily low rates near threshold. The difference is explained by different mathematical bifurcations: in type II models, the resting state loses stability through a Hopf bifurcation, while in type I models, it typically disappears through a saddle-node on invariant circle bifurcation. Engineers familiar with nonlinear oscillators will recognize these terms; they describe how a stable equilibrium turns into a limit cycle oscillation as a parameter (here, the injected current) is varied.

Understanding the dynamics: reduction to two dimensions

A four-dimensional system is hard to visualize. Because m is much faster than the other variables, one can approximate m by its steady-state value m_inf(V) at every moment. And because h and n change on similar time scales and are roughly anticorrelated during an action potential, one can approximate h by a linear function of n (for example h is approximately 0.89 - 1.1*n, an approximation discussed by John Rinzel and others). This reduces the HH model to two variables: V (fast) and n (slow).

Two-dimensional systems can be analyzed in the phase plane. One plots the nullclines: the curve where dV/dt = 0 (the V-nullcline), which for neuron models is typically N-shaped (cubic), and the curve where dn/dt = 0 (the n-nullcline), which is a monotonic sigmoid. Their intersection is the resting state. A small perturbation decays back to rest. A large enough perturbation pushes the state past the middle branch of the V-nullcline, and the trajectory makes a large excursion around the nullclines before returning: this is the action potential. Under sustained current, the V-nullcline shifts up, the intersection moves to the middle branch, rest becomes unstable, and the system settles into a limit cycle: repetitive firing.

This geometric picture was developed in the 1960s by Richard FitzHugh, who created a simplified two-variable model with a cubic nullcline, and independently by Jin-ichi Nagumo and colleagues, who built an electronic circuit implementing it with a tunnel diode. The FitzHugh-Nagumo model is:

  dv/dt = v - v^3/3 - w + I
  dw/dt = epsilon * (v + a - b*w)

where v is a voltage-like variable, w is a recovery variable, I is input current, and epsilon is small (so w is slow). It is a relative of the van der Pol oscillator, a classic relaxation oscillator from electronics. For a mechatronics student, this is a good place to see the unity between neurons and circuits: the neuron is a relaxation oscillator with an excitable resting state.

Why the HH model is so important

The HH model is important for several reasons beyond its accuracy for the squid axon.

First, it is mechanistic. Every term corresponds to a physical quantity that can be measured: capacitance, conductances, reversal potentials, gating kinetics. It is not just a description of behavior but an explanation in terms of components.

Second, it is general. The same mathematical framework, with different channels and parameters, is used to model neurons throughout the nervous system, and also heart cells, muscle cells, and endocrine cells. Mammalian neurons have many more types of channels than the squid axon (dozens of potassium channel types, calcium channels, hyperpolarization-activated channels, and so on), and each can be modeled in HH style. Software packages like NEURON and Brian implement this framework.

Third, it made predictions that were later confirmed at the molecular level, such as gating currents and the existence of separate sodium and potassium channels.

Fourth, it is a model of excitability that has inspired mathematicians, physicists, and engineers. The study of excitable media, from heart arrhythmias to chemical waves, uses HH-style reasoning.

Limitations

The HH model is not perfect. Its gating variables are independent, but real sodium channel inactivation is coupled to activation (a channel usually needs to open before it inactivates). Single-channel recordings later showed that the HH particle picture is an approximation of more complex multi-state kinetics, better described by Markov models with many states. The HH equations are deterministic, while real channels open and close randomly; in small neurons or thin axons, this "channel noise" can affect firing. And the model uses the linear (ohmic) current-voltage relation, which is approximate. But as a first description, it remains the standard.

Bridge to AI: from conductance models to activation functions

There is a direct line from the HH model to the activation functions used in AI, through simplification.

1. The HH model has four variables per patch of membrane and produces spikes.
2. Reduced models like FitzHugh-Nagumo keep two variables and the qualitative dynamics.
3. The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model throws out the spike-generating mechanism altogether: the voltage integrates input as a leaky RC circuit (C*dV/dt = -g_L*(V - E_L) + I), and when V reaches a threshold, a spike is recorded and V is reset. The LIF model was introduced in early form by Louis Lapicque in 1907 (well before HH), long before the mechanism was understood.
4. If you compute the firing rate of an LIF or HH neuron as a function of constant input current, you get the "f-I curve" (frequency versus current). It is zero below threshold and increasing above it. In rate-based neural network models, this f-I curve is used as the activation function. Its shape motivates the sigmoid (saturating at high input, as refractoriness limits maximum firing rate) and the ReLU (zero below threshold, roughly linear above).

So when a deep learning engineer writes y = max(0, x), they are using a cartoon of the f-I curve of a neuron, which is itself a summary of the HH dynamics. The HH f-I curve we computed above is not continuous at threshold (it jumps from 0 to about 56 spikes per second), which is a type II behavior; type I neurons have a continuous f-I curve that starts at zero, closer to the shape of a ReLU or its smooth variants such as softplus.

Second, there is a growing interest in AI in using biologically detailed models as "teachers" or targets. For example, researchers have trained deep networks to emulate the input-output behavior of detailed biophysical models of cortical neurons, and found that it can take a surprisingly deep network to reproduce one detailed neuron with dendrites accurately. One frequently cited study by David Beniaguev, Idan Segev, and Michael London (published in Neuron in 2021) reported that a temporally convolutional network with several layers was needed to capture the input-output function of a detailed model of a cortical pyramidal neuron, largely because of nonlinear NMDA receptor-dependent processes in the dendrites. This suggests that a single biological neuron may be computationally much richer than a single artificial unit.

Summary

- The HH model consists of a membrane equation with sodium, potassium, and leak currents, plus three gating variables m, h, and n.
- Sodium conductance is g_Na_max * m^3 * h; potassium conductance is g_K_max * n^4.
- Each gating variable obeys dx/dt = alpha_x(V)*(1 - x) - beta_x(V)*x, equivalently relaxing to x_inf(V) with time constant tau_x(V).
- Fast sodium activation provides positive feedback; slower sodium inactivation and potassium activation provide negative feedback.
- A simple simulation shows threshold behavior, single spikes, and repetitive firing beginning at a nonzero rate (type II excitability), with spikes peaking near +40 mV.
- Reduced models (FitzHugh-Nagumo, integrate-and-fire) connect the HH model to relaxation oscillators and to the activation functions of artificial neural networks.
